translation: Shall we get started then?

Here we will explain basic chess techniques as
you solve…
…a chess puzzle.

For basic rules and explanations of chess,
please refer to Itsuki Koizumi's puzzle.
From now on, we will assume you understand…
…how each of the pieces move.

Before we start learning techniques, we'll
first explain "gaining advantage.”

There are six types of chess piece in total,
and they each move and attack differently.

Although in either case you're only losing one
piece, there's a big difference in…
…losing a pawn compared to losing a queen.

In chess, each piece is assigned a strength
value.

By totaling up the strength values of all the
pieces in play, you can get a broad idea…

…of which player has the advantage or
disadvantage.

In other words, if when taking or losing a
piece the total value of your pieces…

…overtakes your opponent's, you can assume
that you have the advantage.

It's important to plan your strategies such
that you lose as few points as possible…

…and take as many points from your
opponent as possible.

However, victory in chess is not about taking
as many of your opponent's pieces…

…as possible, it's about checkmating your
opponent, so don't concern yourself with it…

…too much, or you'll have the rug pulled out
from under your feet.

Even if a pawn takes your queen, as long as
you can checkmate your opponent…
…that's all that matters to win!

Take a look at the strength points of each
piece.

As you can see from the diagram, the king is
valued as infinite, as it cannot be taken.

The value goes down from the queen, to the
rook, to the bishop and the knight…
…and then to the pawn.

Let's take a look at an example on the
bottom screen.

If a knight is taken with a queen, and then
the knight is taken in return…

…the opponent loses 9 points of strength,
while you lose 3 points.

This means that in total, you gain a 6 point
advantage.
